In [[mathematics]], a '''Gårding domain''' is a concept in the [[representation theory]] of [[topological group]]s. The concept is named after the [[mathematician]] [[Lars Gårding]].

Let ''G'' be a topological group and let ''U'' be a [[strongly continuous]] [[unitary representation]] of ''G'' in a [[separable space|separable]] [[Hilbert space]] ''H''. Denote by '''''g''''' the family of all [[one-parameter subgroup]]s of ''G''. For each ''δ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;{&nbsp;''δ''(''t'')&nbsp;|&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''&nbsp;}&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''''g''''', let ''U''(''δ'') denote the [[self-adjoint]] [[Generator (mathematics)|generator]] of the unitary one-parameter subgroup {&nbsp;''U''(''δ''(''t''))&nbsp;|&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''&nbsp;}. A '''Gårding domain''' for ''U'' is a [[linear subspace]] of ''H'' that is ''U''(''g'')- and ''U''(''δ'')-[[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] for all ''g''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''G'' and ''δ''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''''g''''' and is also a domain of [[Self-adjoint operator|essential self-adjointness]] for ''U''

Gårding showed in 1947 that, if ''G'' is a [[Lie group]], then a Gårding domain for ''U'' consisting of infinitely differentiable vectors exists for each continuous unitary representation of ''G''. In 1961, Kats extended this result to arbitrary [[locally compact space|locally compact]] topological groups. However, these results do not extend easily to the non-locally compact case because of the lack of a [[Haar measure]] on the group. In 1996, Danilenko proved the following result for groups ''G'' that can be written as the [[inductive limit]] of an increasing sequence ''G''<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;''G''<sub>2</sub>&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;... of locally compact [[second countable]] [[subgroup]]s:

Let ''U'' be a strongly continuous unitary representation of ''G'' in a separable Hilbert space ''H''. Then there exist a separable [[nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Montel space]] ''F'' and a continuous, [[bijection|bijective]], [[linear map]] ''J''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''F''&nbsp;→&nbsp;''H'' such that
* the [[dual space]] of ''F'', denoted by ''F''<sup>∗</sup>, has the structure of a separable [[Fréchet space]] with respect to the strong topology on the dual pairing (''F''<sup>∗</sup>,&nbsp;''F'');
* the image of ''J'', im(''J''), is [[dense set|dense]] in ''H'';
* for all ''g''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''G'', ''U''(''g'')(im(''J''))&nbsp;=&nbsp;im(''J'');
* for all ''δ''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''''g''''', ''U''(''δ'')(im(''J''))&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;im(''J'') and im(''J'') is a domain of essential self-adjointness for ''U''(''δ'');
* for all ''g''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''G'', ''J''<sup>&minus;1</sup>''U''(''g'')''J'' is a continuous linear map from ''F'' to itself;
* moreover, the map ''G''&nbsp;→&nbsp;Lin(''F'';&nbsp;''F'') taking ''g'' to ''J''<sup>&minus;1</sup>''U''(''g'')''J'' is continuous with respect to the topology on ''G'' and the [[weak operator topology]] on Lin(''F'';&nbsp;''F'').

The space ''F'' is known as a '''strong Gårding space''' for ''U'' and im(''J'') is called a '''strong Gårding domain''' for ''U''. Under the above assumptions on ''G'' there is a natural [[Lie algebra]] structure on ''G'', so it makes sense to call '''''g''''' the Lie algebra of ''G''.
